questions.question: Write any two functions of soil organic matter. / [CO3] [2x5 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Functions of Organic Matter:
  • • Physical: Improves soil structure, reducing compaction, and enhancing aeration and water infiltration.
  • • Chemical: Increases Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC), allowing soil to store nutrients (like N, P, K) and
  • improving nutrient availability to plants.
  • • Biological: Acts as the primary energy source and habitat for soil organisms (bacteria, fungi, earthworms)
  • • Environmental: Enhances carbon storage (sequestration), which mitigates climate change and helps build
  • resilient soil structure that reduces erosion by water and wind.
  • Benefits to Soil Health:
  • • Water Management: Acts like a sponge, holding water, which increases drought resistance.
  • • Soil Nutrient Management: Provides a slow-release, steady supply of nutrients, reducing the need for heavy
  • chemical fertilizer application.
  • • Soil Structure: Darkens soil, increases aeration and reduces erosion.

questions.question: What is organic manures ? Briefly describe classification of orgnic manures with examples. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Organic manure is a natural fertilizer derived from decaying plant and animal waste, used to enrich soil
  • fertility and provide nutrients to plants. It is made from sources like animal dung, crop residues, and kitchen
  • waste, and it improves soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
  • -Classification of organic manures
  • Bulky organic manure
  • Bulky organic manure refers to materials of plant and animal origin that are applied in large quantities due to
  • their low nutrient concentration, but high organic matter content. Common examples include farmyard manure
  • (FYM), compost, and green manure. These manures improve soil structure, water retention, and nutrient
  • availability.
  • • Farmyard manure (FYM): A mixture of cow dung, urine, and other organic matter, usually collected and
  • stored in a roofed enclosure.
  • • Compost: Decomposed organic materials like yard waste, food scraps, and other plant -based matter.
  • • Green manure: Plants grown specifically to be incorporated into the soil while still green to add organic
  • matter and nutrients.
  • • Other types: Sewage sludge and seaweed can also be considered bulky organic manures, though they may
  • require special treatment before use to remove harmful components like pathogens and heavy metals.
  • Concentrated organic manure
  • Concentrated organic manure is a type of nutrient-rich fertilizer derived from animal and plant sources,
  • containing a higher percentage of plant nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium compared to bulky
  • organic manures. Examples include oil cakes, blood meal, bone meal, and fish manure.
  • • Oil cakes: The by product of extracting oil from seeds, such as groundnut cake and neem cake.
  • • Blood meal: Dried and powdered animal blood.
  • • Bone meal: Crushed animal bones, rich in phosphorus and calcium.
  • • Fish manure: Processed fish waste, also known as fish emulsion or fish meal.
  • • Bird guano: Dried droppings from birds or bats.
  • • Horn and hoof meal: Ground horns and hooves of animals.

questions.question: Explain about soil profile with horizons. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• SOIL PROFILE
  • A soil profile is a vertical cross-section of the soil that reveals its various layers, or horizons. These layers, such
  • as the topsoil (A horizon), subsoil (B horizon), and parent material (C horizon), have distinct characteristics in
  • color, texture, and chemical composition that are formed by soil-forming processes. A soil profile is used to
  • understand the soil's properties for agriculture and conservation.
  • The layers of soil
  • Mature soil is made up of different horizontal layers, called horizons, which are visible in a vertical cross-
  • section called a soil profile.
  • • O-Horizon (Organic Layer): The uppermost layer, composed of dead plant and animal matter in various stages
  • of decomposition. partially decayed organic matter.
  • • A-Horizon (Topsoil): A mineral layer rich with accumulated humus. This is the dark, nutrient-rich layer where
  • most plant roots and soil organisms are found.
  • • E Horizon (Eluviated): A layer of mineral soil that has lost some of its material through leaching (washing
  • out).
  • • B-Horizon (Subsoil): The layer below the topsoil. It contains less organic matter but accumulates clay, iron,
  • and other materials leached from the layers above.
  • • C-Horizon (Parent Material): The unconsolidated material below the subsoil, which is only slightly
  • weathered.
  • • R Horizon (Bedrock): The layer of unweathered, consolidated rock that lies beneath the soil.

questions.solution_html:
• CONTROL OF WIND EROSION
  • Vegetative Cover: vegetative cover discourages soil blowing by winds
  • Mulching: mulching has ability to be effective in controlling wind erosion.
  • Rough Surface: Wind is more effective on smooth surface than on rough surface.
  • Organic Matter: This is increasing the stability of the soil structure, for improving water-holding capacity of
  • the soil and for building up its fertility.
  • Regulating Grazing: Probably the most important cause of wind erosion is overgrazing There must be grazing
  • regulations ( prevent over grazing)
  • Wind Break and Shelterbelt: Trees and shrubs, commonly planted in rows at right angles to the preventing
  • winds are called shelterbelts.
  • ➢ Control of Water Erosion
  • There are two methods for the control or management of land eroded by water: (a . Agronomical method, and (b)
  • Mechanical Method.
  • I. Agronomical Method.
  • Growing Cover Crops: crops, such as grass, sunhemp, groundnut are excellent soil protection against erosion
  • by water.
  • Crop Rotation: Growing of two more different crops in sequence in a field for maintaining the soil fertility.
  • Where plants are densely arranged ,it prevent water erosion
  • Mulching: Mulches of different kinds minimise evaporation and increases absorption of moisture /water. It will
  • reduce soil erosion
  • Organic Manures: Incorporation of organic manures in the soil improves the soil structure. Granular and
  • crumby structures increase infiltration and permeability in the soil and conserve soil water.
  • II.Mechanical Methods.
  • • Contour Tillage: On hilly land areas tillage operations and the sowing of crops should be done at right
  • angles manner this will prevent erosion Ploughing is Perpendicular to the slop
  • • Pan Breaking and Sub-soiling: It break the hard pan of the soil and increase infiltration. This increases the
  • water storage capacity of the soil, thus, decreasing run-off and erosion.
  • • Water Harvest: At suitable places like pond and tanks are store rain water.

questions.question: Describe detail about INM with its components and advantages. / [CO3] [15x1 = 15]
questions.solution_html:
• Integrated Nutrient Management (INM)
  • Integrated Nutrient Management (INM) is an approach to agriculture that combines organic, inorganic, and
  • biological nutrient sources to maintain soil fertility and plant productivity while minimizing environmental
  • impact. This involves using a mix of chemical fertilizers, organic manures (like com post and green manure), and
  • biofertilizers to improve soil health and crop yields sustainably.
  • Components of Integrated Nutrient Management
  • The main components of INM are inorganic fertilizers, organic manures, biofertilizers and vermicompost.
